content: Cayston (aztreonam inhalation) is a medication specifically indicated to improve respiratory symptoms in patients with cystic fibrosis (CF) who are infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The recommended dosage is 75 mg inhaled every 8 hours for 28 days, administered using the Altera nebulizer. After completing a 28-day course, the treatment should not be repeated for another 28 days. Doses must be spaced at least 4 hours apart. Prior to administration, a bronchodilator should be used. Short-acting beta agonists should be taken 15 minutes to 4 hours before Cayston, while long-acting beta agonists should be taken 30 minutes to 12 hours prior. If mucolytics are part of the treatment regimen, they should be taken after bronchodilators but before aztreonam. The vials and diluent should be stored refrigerated at 2–8°C (36–46°F). Once removed from refrigeration, they can be stored at room temperature (up to 25°C or 77°F) for up to 28 days. The medication should be used immediately after reconstitution, and only one dose should be reconstituted at a time. Cayston is approved for use in patients aged 7 years and older, with the same dosing regimen as adults. Its safety and efficacy have not been established in children under 7 years of age. Common adverse effects include cough (54%), nasal congestion (16%), wheezing (16%), pharyngolaryngeal pain (12%), fever (13%), chest discomfort (8%), abdominal pain (7%), vomiting (6%), bronchospasm (3%), and rash (2%). Hypersensitivity and allergic reactions have been observed in clinical trials, and treatment should be discontinued if an allergic reaction occurs. Bronchospasm may also occur, and treatment should be stopped if chest tightness develops during nebulizer use. Cayston has been shown to increase FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 second) during the 28-day treatment course. Baseline FEV1 should be considered when evaluating post-treatment changes, as these may be related to pulmonary exacerbations. There is an increased risk of drug-resistant bacteria if the medication is used in the absence of a known Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection. Data on the use of Cayston in pregnant women is insufficient to determine the risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. However, systemic absorption of aztreonam following inhalation is expected to be minimal. Cystic fibrosis during pregnancy may increase the risk of preterm delivery. Following intravenous administration, aztreonam is excreted in human milk at concentrations less than 1% of maternal serum levels. Peak plasma concentrations of aztreonam after a 75 mg inhaled dose are approximately 1% of those observed following a 500 mg intravenous dose. Systemic absorption after inhalation is minimal, and there is no data on the effects of the drug on breastfed infants or milk production. The benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for therapy and any potential adverse effects on the infant or the underlying maternal condition. Pharmacokinetically, the mean sputum concentration of aztreonam after a single dose is 726 mcg/g, with levels of 984 mcg/g, 793 mcg/g, and 715 mcg/g observed 10 minutes after multiple doses on days 1, 14, and 28, respectively. The peak plasma time is approximately 1 hour, with 56% of the drug being protein-bound. Aztreonam is primarily excreted in the urine (60–70%) and to a lesser extent in feces (13–15%). This information is provided for general educational purposes and may vary depending on individual circumstances. For the most current and specific information, consult the applicable healthcare provider or plan.
